title: Affine relative Hom from a finite free affine source
statement:
Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $Y=\operatorname{Spec}C$ be affine $S$-schemes, with $S$-morphisms $Z\to T$ and $Y\to T$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Assume the induced $R$-module $B$ has a basis indexed by $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $m\geq0$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. On $S$-schemes define
$$F(U)=\{(a,b)\mid a:U\to T,\ b:U\times_{a,T}Z\to Y,\ b\text{ is over }T\},$$
with restriction by precomposition with the induced fibre-product map [def-pc-fibre-product]. There exists an affine scheme $M$ over $T$ with a natural bijection $\operatorname{Mor}_S(U,M)\simeq F(U)$ for all $S$-schemes $U$, compatible with the maps to $\operatorname{Mor}_S(U,T)$. No finite-type or finite-presentation assumption on the $R$-algebra $C$ is imposed. The case $m=0$ is included.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine; functor equation-hom-functor in the preceding section.

proof.text: Choose the given basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ of $B$. Take $I$ to be the underlying set of $C$ and let $Q=R[x_i:i\in I]$. Evaluation $\epsilon:Q\to C$, $x_i\mapsto i$, is surjective, since every $i\in C$ is the image of $x_i$. Put $K=\ker\epsilon$ and index relations $f_k$ by all $k\in K$, with $f_k=k$. Then $C\cong Q/K$: the inverse of the induced map sends $c$ to the class of any $q$ with $\epsilon(q)=c$, independently of the choice because differences lie in $K$. Addition, multiplication and constants are preserved by this inverse. This gives a presentation with no finiteness restriction on either index set.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: Put $P=R[a_{ij}:i\in I,1\leq j\leq m]$. Polynomial evaluation defines $\Psi:Q\to P\otimes_R B$ by $x_i\mapsto\sum_j a_{ij}\otimes e_j$. By base change of the given basis, each $\Psi(f_k)$ has a unique expression $\sum_j c_{kj}\otimes e_j$ with $c_{kj}\in P$. Let $J$ be the ideal of $P$ generated by these coefficients and put $D=P/J$, with quotient $q:P\to D$. Thus $M=\operatorname{Spec}D$ is an affine scheme, with structural map $M\to T$ induced by $R\to D$, and hence an $S$-scheme.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: Fix any commutative $R$-algebra $A$. A homomorphism $u:P\to A$ gives an $R$-algebra map $\theta_u:Q\to A\otimes_R B$ by $x_i\mapsto\sum_j u(a_{ij})\otimes e_j$. The maps $\theta_u$ and $(u\otimes1)\Psi$ agree on each generator and on $R$, hence are equal. Consequently $\theta_u(f_k)=\sum_j u(c_{kj})\otimes e_j$. The base-changed basis is linearly independent, so all these values vanish exactly when every $u(c_{kj})$ is zero, equivalently $J\subseteq\ker u$. A map kills an ideal generated by a family precisely when it kills each generator: every element of that ideal is a finite sum of multiples of those generators.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: It follows that $R$-algebra maps $D\to A$ correspond bijectively to $R$-algebra maps $C\to A\otimes_R B$. Explicitly, $v:D\to A$ gives $u=vq$; step 3 makes $\theta_u$ kill $K$, so $[f]\mapsto\theta_u(f)$ is a well-defined algebra map $Q/K\to A\otimes_R B$. Conversely, given $h:C\to A\otimes_R B$, write the unique expansions $h(\overline{x}_i)=\sum_j\alpha_{ij}\otimes e_j$. Define $u(a_{ij})=\alpha_{ij}$ by polynomial evaluation. The equality $\theta_u=h\epsilon$ follows on generators, so step 3 shows $u(J)=0$. The formula $v([p])=u(p)$ is well-defined and gives $D\to A$. Both constructions are inverse, by uniqueness of basis coefficients and polynomial evaluation. They commute with every $R$-algebra map $t:A\to A'$: the coefficients become $t(\alpha_{ij})$, so the corresponding maps become $tv$ and $(t\otimes1)h$.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: For $A=D$, the identity of $D$ therefore gives $h_{\rm univ}:C\to D\otimes_R B$. The affine fibre-product formula and affine spectrum correspondence turn this into a $T$-morphism $b_{\rm univ}:M\times_T Z\to Y$. Pulling it back along a morphism $U\to M$ gives a natural map $\Phi_U:\operatorname{Mor}_T(U,M)\to\operatorname{Mor}_T(U\times_T Z,Y)$ for every $T$-scheme $U$. If $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, affine duality identifies $\Phi_U$ with the bijection of step 4. The identification respects pullback: on coordinate rings the induced map of fibre products is $t\otimes1$, since it has the required restrictions to both tensor factors; uniqueness in the tensor universal property proves the assertion.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: For an arbitrary $T$-scheme $U$ and $b:U\times_TZ\to Y$, choose an affine open cover $(U_l)$ of $U$. Step 5 gives a unique $f_l:U_l\to M$ representing $b$ there. On every affine open $V\subset U_l\cap U_{l'}$, naturality and affine injectivity give $f_l|_V=f_{l'}|_V$. Such $V$ cover the intersection, so uniqueness in morphism gluing gives equality on the whole intersection. Glue the $f_l$ to $f:U\to M$. Its composite to $T$ equals the structure map because this holds on the cover. The inverse images of the $U_l$ under $U\times_TZ\to U$ form an open cover, on which $\Phi_U(f)=b$; gluing uniqueness gives equality globally. If two $f$ give the same $b$, affine injectivity and gluing uniqueness give their equality. Thus $\Phi_U$ is bijective, and its naturality for all $T$-morphisms follows from its definition as pullback of $b_{\rm univ}$. No affine-intersection assumption on $U$ was used.

source.place: Tag 05Y6, lemma-hom-from-finite-free-into-affine, proof; the omitted details are written out.

proof.text: Finally, an $S$-morphism $f:U\to M$ has a uniquely determined composite $a:U\to T$, and is then a $T$-morphism for that structure on $U$. Apply step 6 separately for each $a$. This identifies $f$ with the pair $(a,\Phi_{(U,a)}(f))$ in $F(U)$; the inverse uses the unique map supplied by step 6. Pullback preserves $a$ by composition and preserves the second entry by the fibre-product universal property, proving the claimed naturality on $S$-schemes and compatibility with $\operatorname{Mor}_S(U,T)$. For $m=0$, $B$ is the zero ring, $P=R$, there are no coefficients, $J=0$ and $M=T$. Every $U\times_T Z$ is empty: on each affine chart its coordinate ring is $A\otimes_R0=0$. There is exactly one map from it to $Y$, as also given by the empty basis in step 4. Thus the same bijection includes rank zero, even for nonzero $C$.
